title: Neptune Analytics - CUDA RTC lock + KV-cache stall deep dive
summary: Deep technical review of recurring CUDA RTC lockups causing GPU stalls and KV-cache saturation during mixed seq throughput. Discussed root-cause hypotheses (driver preemption, async kernel scheduling, prefetch throttling), short-term mitigations (aggressive kvcache backoff, request sharding, smaller batch windows), and long-term fixes (runtime watchdog, kernel selector tweaks, driver knob matrix). Agreed next steps: Redwood to run instrumented repro with tuned driver/RT settings, share trace collection script, Neptune to provide small repro trace and priority logs, align on pilot test window.
action_items: Jordan Blake: Share instrumented repro harness and driver/RT config matrix by 2026-09-17
Ethan Liu: Upload a 30s perf trace + dmesg and nvstats dump from failing host by 2026-09-18
Priya Desai: Run controlled repro with kvcache backoff enabled and send results by 2026-09-20
Zoe Kim: Approve temporary SSH access for Redwood SE on 1 test node (window 2026-09-19 morning)
next_steps: Redwood to run instrumented run on customer's repro image and share flame/trace
Customer to provide repro trace and driver versions; Redwood to test driver 535 vs 545 matrix
Schedule 1h follow-up on 2026-09-22 to review instrumented results and decide pilot changes
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-15
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~70 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood Support), Mina (Product), Carlos (Neptune Head of ML Infra), Zoe (Neptune SRE), Ethan (ML Eng), Anya (CTO)

Summary (auto): Discussed recurring GPU stalls that look like CUDA runtime locks plus KV-cache saturation when Neptune runs mixed sequence workloads. Went through hypotheses, quick mitigations and a plan for instrumented repro.

[00:00:05] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm seeing we have the infra folks here, so maybe quick intros then jump in?
[00:00:12] Carlos: yeah Carlos here, I run our infra for models, thanks, gonna hand off to Zoe on the SRE details after intros.
[00:00:16] Zoe: yep, hi all, we've been chasing these intermittent stalls for two weeks, host-level gpu lockups then long tails on latency.
[00:00:23] Priya: thanks, can you summarize the most recent failure pattern first — seq lengths, batch sizes, model, quant?
[00:00:30] Zoe: sure — it's a 13B model, quant int8 dynamic, typical seq 512 prompt + 512 generation for a chunk, concurrent traffic mixes: short requests (<=64) + long (>512) sometimes bursty. Batching window is 50ms, batch size peaks 24 on our 4xA800 nodes. We see transient OOMs then host tracing shows CUDA driver reporting "RTC lock" or long kernel enqueue stalls around 90s.
[00:00:47] Priya: ok that matches earlier notes — sometimes driver-level preemption issues show as RTC stalls. Do you have nv-hostengine logs, nvidia-smi log?
[00:00:54] Zoe: we pulled dmesg and journald, we also grabbed the nvidia bugreport, and a short perf trace. We'll upload after the call.
[00:01:01] Jordan: perfect — high level, Priya and Luis will lead the runtime instrumentation. We want to understand if it's pure memory pressure (kvcache inflation + quant decoding) or scheduler/driver preemption.
[00:01:12] Ethan: quick note — we've tried increasing batch window to 100ms and it actually made the tail worse; latency p50 improved but p99 spiked. So batching tradeoff is real.
[00:01:21] Priya: yep, that's classic — increasing window helps throughput but can amplify kvcache demand and leads to longer active token life and memory pressure; if a kernel blocks, other requests pile up.
[00:01:30] Zoe: we also saw CUDA errors like "invalid device context" occasionally in the runtime logs, which is worrying.
[00:01:36] Luis: sometimes the postmortem logs have mixed syscall traces, so it's not always a single consistent failure mode.

[00:02:12] Priya: can I walk through our hypothesis tree — one: kvcache saturation. Two: kernel scheduling/preemption/driver hang. Three: async prefetch race when quantized kernels hit memory boundary. Four: host-side scheduler and watchdog misconfigured under on-prem constraints. Thoughts?
[00:02:29] Carlos: all of the above sounds plausible. We're also running kernel 535.86 or similar, we tried a hotfix kernel from vendor but haven't seen improvement.
[00:02:37] Priya: got it. For kvcache saturation we need to look at per-request kv footprint and hit/miss pattern. With mixed seq workloads, short requests reuse kv then long ones expand it. If batches interleave growth and eviction, you can get transient double allocations.
[00:02:51] Ethan: we have telemetry that shows kvcache size grows linearly across a window of ~8s under burst, then a spike where active allocations jump 20%. That's when the OOM or stall triggers.
[00:03:02] Priya: good telemetry to have — we usually recommend prefix caching limit + aggressive eviction policy in those mixed workloads. Audience: are you using our prefix-level cache config or just local kvcache?
[00:03:11] Zoe: it's local kvcache with the default LRU. We haven't enabled prefix caching because of TTL concerns.
[00:03:16] Priya: ok LRU defaults can be brittle under bursty, mixed sequences. One mitigation: set kvcache.max_entries smaller, enable per-prefix TTL for ephemeral sessions, and enable backpressure where incoming requests trigger kvcache backoff if memory crosses threshold. That buys breathing room.
[00:03:33] Carlos: what's the expected perf cost of aggressive eviction? We worry about repeated recompute on chat sessions.
[00:03:38] Priya: there is a cost — some recompute/latency tradeoff. But it's cheaper than full host OOM or driver stall that takes node offline for minutes. You can also use targeted eviction for long, low-value prefixes.

[00:04:05] Anya: from a product perspective, we can't tolerate glitchy behavior during our demo windows; we need a mitigation that is safe and reversible.
[00:04:12] Jordan: absolutely — we'll propose a canary: enable kvcache backoff on 10% of traffic in non-prod, measure p99 and failover behavior.

[00:04:35] Priya: second thread — driver/kernel scheduling. Some environments show slow cudaMemcpy or kernel launch latencies under certain driver versions. If driver preemption is delayed, GPU kernels can block longer than expected. Sometimes it's a streaming lock (RTC) where runtime API serialises CUDA launches. We'll check for two things: long synchronous host calls and kernel launch queue depth.
[00:04:55] Ethan: how would Redwood instrument that in our environment? We're sensitive about installing agents.
[00:05:00] Luis: we can run a lightweight tracing harness that uses NVTX and the CUDA profiling API to emit per-kernel timestamps into a gzipped trace. No invasive kernel changes; we just need a short maintenance window to run the repro.
[00:05:10] Zoe: willing to do one node, morning 9–11 PDT if Redwood aligns.
[00:05:14] Priya: great — we'll coordinate. We'll also try the repro under two driver versions (535.x vs 545.x) and with/without TCC (if applicable). Also validate with and without MIG partitioning if you had that configured.

[00:05:43] Carlos: we're not using MIG, it's full device. We do have an on-prem security constraint: KMS access is restricted and we can't share images, so Redwood will need to run testing remotely against a repro node with temporary SSH access.
[00:05:56] Jordan: noted — we'll request ephemeral access just for the repro run.

[00:06:08] Priya: third hypothesis — quantization memory behavior. Some int8 kernels have larger working memory when doing per-block dequant/requant, causing transient spikes. On certain GPUs that memory is allocated per-kernel and can bloat under higher batch size.
[00:06:20] Ethan: that would explain why bumping batch window made p99 worse. We are using dynamic quant int8 with per-channel scales.
[00:06:26] Priya: ok, short mitigation: force dequant streaming smaller tile sizes or fall back to int16 path for long sequence generation when memory thresholds hit. Redwood runtime supports kernel selector overrides.
[00:06:36] Anya: are those runtime selectors safe? We'd prefer non-invasive config changes over code changes.
[00:06:40] Priya: the selector is a config flag, you can pin a given kernel profile for a model/route. It's reversible. We'll provide suggested profiles after the instrumented run.

[00:07:02] Zoe: earlier you mentioned watchdogs — can Redwood runtime proactively kill long-running kernels to avoid whole-node stall? We tried host watchdog but it sometimes destabilizes the node.
[00:07:11] Luis: we do have a runtime watchdog that can preempt and fallback to smaller model variant or return a graceful 503 so other requests are not impacted. The trick is tuning the threshold — too aggressive kills good work, too lax and you get node-level stalls.
[00:07:23] Priya: for this customer we'd recommend: 1) enable graceful kernel timeout at 45s, 2) on timeout, trigger kvcache trim + route subsequent requests to small variant for 30s, 3) emit telemetry and roll a short backoff. That avoids full eviction and allows fast recovery.
[00:07:37] Carlos: 45s seems high — our kernel stalls were near 90s; is there risk of spurious timeouts?
[00:07:44] Priya: threshold chosen to minimize false positives; but we'll tune after seeing traces.

[00:08:05] Jordan: let's talk about retry semantics — currently Neptune retries at application layer after a 10s timeout, we suspect that contributes to stacking.
[00:08:13] Ethan: yes we have simple exponential retries with no jitter; 3 attempts. Under node stalls, retries amplify load.
[00:08:18] Priya: recommended pattern: use idempotency keys + client-side jittered retry with increasing backoff and global concurrency cap. On the platform side, Redwood can return a specific Retry-After and a transient error class that signals clients to back off more aggressively.
[00:08:31] Jordan: we'll include suggested header semantics and sample client logic as part of the deliverables.

[00:08:52] Zoe: question — we run in VPC with limited egress; does Redwood need control plane access to collect traces?
[00:08:58] Jordan: no control plane changes required; Redwood SEs will need ephemeral SSH to a node or you can upload traces to the secure bucket. We'll provide upload scripts that don't require outbound egress if you'd prefer.

[00:09:20] Priya: let's go deeper into one of the repros you shared — the perf trace shows a large cluster of kernel-launch stalls around t=182s where a long generation hits and then we see several host-side memcpy stalls. Could be host-to-device contention.
[00:09:33] Ethan: yep that's the time window where p99 skyrockets and the node becomes unresponsive to new RPCs for ~2 minutes.
[00:09:40] Priya: do you get any NVLINK errors or PCIe resets in the kernel ring?
[00:09:44] Zoe: we saw a single PCIe error in dmesg a week ago, but it was chalked up to bad PSU at the time.
[00:09:50] Luis: even a single transient PCIe error can exacerbate driver state; tracing will show whether the runtime enters an error-recovery path.

[00:10:12] Priya: one more instrument: capture per-stream semaphores and kernel durations with NVTX ranges, and set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 for repro so we get native async behavior. Also we'll test with CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 to compare synchronous behaviour — differences can reveal scheduling races.
[00:10:30] Ethan: ok we'll run both.

[00:10:45] Anya: what about model sharding or splitting long requests to reduce kv pressure?
[00:10:51] Priya: split-at-token is possible but requires application changes — runtime-level streaming splitting is trickier but possible as a temporary shim. We'll include a small adapter you can use as a test.

[00:11:12] Carlos: in terms of risk, what's the fastest lever?
[00:11:15] Priya: immediate: kvcache.max_entries reduction + backoff + client retry tuning. Short term: run instrumented traces vs driver versions; mid-term: kernel selector tweaks and runtime watchdog.

[00:11:29] Jordan: let's list concrete next steps and owners — (we iterated this earlier in action items). Also we'll schedule the repro window for 2026-09-19 16:00 UTC (that's 9am PDT) if that works for you.
[00:11:41] Zoe: that works. We'll open a ticket for temporary SSH access.

[00:12:05] Priya: a couple more quick clarifying questions from the SE side — are you doing burst traffic from multiple hosts targeting same model replica or is traffic funneled?
[00:12:13] Ethan: it's from multiple app servers; we use a fronting LB and traffic tries to spread but sometimes affinity keeps hits on same replica.
[00:12:21] Priya: affinity + long sequences = hot spot replication of kvcache. For hot prefixes we recommend either sticky routing to a replica with warm cache or distribute and set smaller per-replica caches.

[00:12:38] Carlos: can Redwood route by prefix? We have a small number of enterprise customers that need hard affinity.
[00:12:44] Jordan: yes the runtime supports route-level affinity; we can map user-id hash to replica or a session sticky token. We'll include config examples.

[00:12:56] Zoe: any security concerns about letting Redwood run the instrumented repro? We have strict audit requirements.
[00:13:02] Luis: we'll use ephemeral creds, and all commands are scripted — we'll produce a signed one-time command manifest for audit.

[00:13:15] Ethan: I'm worried about kernel selector flips causing perf regressions mid-run.
[00:13:19] Priya: understandable — we'll run selectors in a conservatively isolated canary and present a clear revert path. Also we'll snapshot current config.

[00:13:33] Anya: cost question — will switching to smaller kernel tiles or int16 increase token cost?
[00:13:38] Priya: it can increase compute cost slightly; we'll quantify with bench runs. Usually tradeoff is 5–15% increase vs avoiding multi-minute node drop and OOM.

[00:13:55] Jordan: ok time check — we have about 40 minutes left; Priya and Luis will propose exact command list for the repro and the driver matrix. We'll also produce a small KB on kvcache knobs and suggested sample configs.

[00:14:12] Priya: quick runbook sketch I'll send: 1) collect nv-hostengine and nvidia-smi loop (30s), 2) collect NVTX-instrumented run, 3) enable kvcache backoff in non-prod, 4) test driver 535 vs 545, 5) run 2x short-burst tests and capture traces.
[00:14:28] Zoe: good. One more Q: what logs do you need for the node? We can provide journald, dmesg, and runtime logs.
[00:14:34] Luis: the list: dmesg, /var/log/messages or journald export, nvidia-bug-report, runtime-profiler trace, and the transaction ids for the failing requests. Also the system coredump if present.

[00:14:50] Carlos: we'll gather and upload after the call.

[00:15:03] Jordan: anything else from the customer side?
[00:15:06] Ethan: just that we want to avoid service disruption; if you need to change kernel selectors in prod we'll request a maintenance window.
[00:15:11] Jordan: understood. We'll limit changes to canaries and non-prod first.

[00:15:20] Priya: final note — we'll also check if your model variant supports KV cache compression options; some models allow compressed kvcache which reduces memory but costs CPU. Worth evaluating.
[00:15:30] Zoe: ok please add that to the KB.

[00:15:45] Jordan: recap: Redwood shares repro harness + driver matrix; customer uploads trace and grants ephemeral access; run scheduled 2026-09-19 16:00 UTC; follow-up meeting 2026-09-22 to review findings. Action items and owners will be emailed.
[00:15:58] Anya: thanks everyone.
[00:16:02] Jordan: thanks — we'll close the notes and send the artifacts.

[00:16:10] (call continues with quick Q&A about packaging but mostly admin — trimmed)

[00:25:00] (end of main discussion; notes truncated to keep transcript focused on technical flow)
